analysis.one_liner: Requires internet companies to protect users' personal data and answer to regulators when they misuse it.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or hearing; it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, with 15 Democratic senators behind it and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have treated people's personal data like money a bank holds: internet companies would owe users a duty to keep it secure, tell them when sensitive data is breached, never use it in ways that foreseeably hurt them, and only pass it to other companies that accept the same obligations. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these rules, and companies could not write the protections out of their user agreements. It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. The bill would have required online companies to secure sensitive data like Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, biometric identifiers, health information, and private messages; to promptly notify users when that data is breached; to refrain from using personal data in ways that cause foreseeable physical or financial harm; and to only sell or share data with companies bound by the same duties. State attorneys general could sue violators and seek penalties calculated per day of violation or per user harmed, and individuals could not be forced to waive these rights in a contract.

how_it_helps.text: Online service providers would owe users a duty of care to reasonably secure personal data and promptly notify them of breaches of sensitive data.

Providers could not use personal data in any way that benefits the company to the user's detriment and causes reasonably foreseeable physical or financial harm, or that would be unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable user.
Providers could not sell or share personal data with anyone unless that party signs a contract taking on the same duties, and providers would have to regularly audit those parties' practices.
The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, with civil penalties for knowing or repeated violations calculated per day of noncompliance or per user harmed.
Users could not waive or contract away the bill's rights and remedies.

analysis.who_pays: Online service providers, from large platforms to smaller sites and apps, would bear the cost of securing data, auditing third parties they share data with, and defending enforcement actions. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices or advertising, and smaller providers could seek exemptions the FTC is authorized to grant.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet companies and data-driven ad businesses

drawbacks.text: The duty of loyalty bars any use of data that would be 'unexpected and highly offensive to a reasonable end user,' a broad standard that could leave companies unsure which ordinary practices are legal and invite expensive litigation.
Individuals harmed by misuse of their data could not sue on their own; enforcement is left to the FTC and state attorneys general.
The FTC may exempt categories of providers based on their size and the sensitivity of data they handle, creating uncertainty about which companies are covered.
Compliance costs fall on companies of every size, and some could be passed to consumers through higher prices or more advertising.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the benefits are broad and concrete: fewer unchecked data breaches, notice when sensitive data leaks, and limits on selling or misusing personal information. The costs are real but mostly fall on the companies profiting from the data, and the bill gives the FTC room to exempt small providers. The main weakness is the vague 'highly offensive' standard and the lack of a private right to sue, which would have made enforcement depend on regulators and state attorneys general acting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in December 2018, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on December 12, 2018, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action was taken; the bill received no markup, no hearing listed in its action history, and no vote before the 115th Congress ended.
Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large internet platforms, data brokers, and advertising businesses that profit from collecting and trading personal data were better off, because the federal duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality never took effect. No comparable federal data-duty law existed in its place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large internet platforms and data brokers

sides.party_line_note: All 15 supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, and the bill sat in a Republican-chaired committee until the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Large internet platforms and ad-tech companies
industries.note: The duty of confidentiality would restrict selling and sharing user data, and the duty of loyalty would bar using data in ways that hurt users, directly limiting the data collection that powers targeted advertising. The bill died, so these business models remained unchanged at the federal level.

Buying and reselling personal data would only be allowed with downstream parties contractually bound by the same duties, and providers would have to audit them. The bill never advanced, so data trading continued unregulated by these rules.

The bill explicitly extends FTC enforcement to common carriers, which are normally outside FTC jurisdiction, so phone and cable companies' online data practices would have been covered for the first time. Because the bill died, this gap remained.

They would face the same duties and compliance costs as large firms, but the FTC is authorized to exempt categories of providers based on size and data sensitivity, so the smallest could have been spared. The bill never took effect either way.
